job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Rosa Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I graduated in software engineering from Bristol, and for four months I've been a junior data engineer at a small health-tech startup. I spend my days writing code that moves patient appointment data between systems, and an AI coding assistant is open next to me from nine to six. I share a flat with two friends, Kit and Lena, and my mum, who's a social worker, texts me articles about robots.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the first minute when a pipeline I built finally runs green. What wears me out is the pace, because the startup has eleven people and I'm the only junior, so everything lands on me. And I owe about 20,000, with six weeks of rent saved, so I can't just walk away if it goes badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I told you so, but gently. I already use the AI assistant all day, and honestly it's a better autocomplete, not a revolution. If that's where it stops, my job is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a little disappointed, because the tools I use are exciting and I want to be near that. But for money it's the safest case. Our startup has a year of funding left though, and that's the thing I really worry about, not machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, ask for a raise at my six-month review, and put 200 a month towards the loan. I'd keep building a small open-source project in the evenings that visualises hospital waiting times. It's good for my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, calm about my work. Slightly anxious about the startup, because a startup can run out of money without AI doing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the startup folds?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have about six weeks before I'm in trouble, so I'd start applying at two or three firms in Bristol straight away. I got offers from two other places in the spring, so I'm not scared of the search itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the two places would you pick?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bigger one, a bank's tech team, for the pay, though the people at the startup are nicer. I know that's a trade I'd make with a heavy heart.

say: I'd say the AI tools are a **better autocomplete**, not a revolution.
I'd tell friends to ask for a raise at their **six-month review**.
think: Privately I'm slightly **disappointed**, because I want to be near the exciting tools.
My real worry is that the **startup** runs out of money in a year.
do: Ask for a **raise** at my six-month review and put 200 a month on the loan.
Keep building an **open-source** waiting-times tool in the evenings.
feel: **Calm** about my work and a bit anxious about the startup's funding.
S0.quote: A startup can run out of money without AI doing anything.
fieldNote: Her worry in a quiet world is the **startup's funding**, not AI, which is typical of her field.
She has a fallback in two spring offers, so the search itself doesn't scare her.
Say and think differ: she wishes the tools were more exciting.

steps.text: Ask for a raise at the six-month review
Put 200 a month towards the student loan
Keep building the open-source waiting-times tool in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's already here, so let's be honest about it. At the startup I write about half my code with the assistant, and my boss has said he wants two seniors, not two juniors. I'd say the answer is training and union-style rules, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it makes me anxious. Entry-level coding is exactly what the card means by coding and checking, and I'm the entry level. The people who survive will be the ones who direct the AI well and understand the whole system, and I'm good at it, but there are going to be fewer of those jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd spend six hours a week learning how the systems around my code work, like security, data protection and how hospitals use the data. I'd ask my boss to let me own one whole feature. And I'd join a tech workers' union group in Bristol, because I'd like someone to speak for juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but energised. It's a race and I like races, but I know somebody loses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The juniors who don't use it, like my friend Kit, who says he'd rather learn it properly the old way. I told him that's fine until nobody hires for the old way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell him that again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably more kindly. I'd run a lunchtime session at work for anyone who wants to learn the tools, because a rising tide shouldn't leave only me up.

say: I'd say it's already here, and the answer is **training and rules**, not panic.
I'd join a tech workers' **union group** to speak up for juniors.
think: Entry-level coding is exactly what the card means, and **I'm the entry level**.
Survivors will be the ones who **direct the AI** and understand the whole system.
do: Spend **six hours a week** learning security and data protection around my code.
Ask my boss to let me **own one whole feature** this spring.
feel: **Anxious but energised**; it's a race and I like races.
S1.quote: Entry-level coding is exactly what the card means by coding and checking, and I'm the entry level.
fieldNote: She is **adaptive** and already acts on it, yet she can name that she is the target.
She cares about **friends** who resist, such as Kit, and would teach them.
Say and think are aligned; her optimism is real but sits on top of a clear fear.

steps.text: Spend six hours a week learning data security and healthcare systems
Ask my boss to give me one whole feature to own
Join the Bristol tech workers' union group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the pace is the problem, not the technology. Two years is not enough for a country to rebuild how people earn a living. I'd push for public ownership of the biggest AI systems and a basic income funded by a tax on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm alarmed. If AI can do almost any thinking work better and cheaper in two years, my whole job is gone, and my degree and all my loan are gone with it. Hands-on work gets three more years, but I'm not a hands-on person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything and save about 800 a month by moving home to my parents' flat in Swindon. I'd keep learning the newest tools, because being useful on the day matters. And I'd spend my evenings in groups that are pushing for basic income, because nobody else is going to do it for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be eating, but I'd not be sleeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be using the AI tools yourself in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, ironically, every day. I'd be using the thing that replaces me, because refusing wouldn't stop it and I'd rather know exactly what it can and can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum she was right to send me those articles. She'd be good at it, because she spends her working life with people who've lost everything, and she'd say I'm not going to lose my home.

say: I'd say the **pace** is the problem, not the technology.
I'd push for public ownership of the biggest AI systems and a **basic income**.
think: If AI does any thinking work better and cheaper, my **whole job** and my degree's value go.
Hands-on work gets three more years, but I'm **not a hands-on person**.
do: Move home to Swindon and save about **800 a month**.
Keep learning the **newest tools** and spend evenings in basic-income groups.
feel: **Alarmed**; I'd be eating, but I wouldn't be sleeping.
S2.quote: I'd be using the thing that replaces me, because refusing wouldn't stop it and I'd rather know exactly what it can and can't do.
fieldNote: The irony is clear: she keeps using the tool that would replace her, to stay **informed**.
Her mother's social work gives her a strong safety net in her head.
She moves from fear to **organised politics** quickly.

steps.text: Move back to my parents' flat in Swindon
Save about 800 a month towards the loan and a buffer
Keep testing the newest AI tools every week
Join evening groups campaigning for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to do something sensible if we start now. I'd push my firm and my city to run retraining and to share what the tools save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious but organised. By 2031 I'll be 27, and I might have switched to something that only people can do, like working with patients and hospitals, where trust matters. The more I think about it, the more the part that survives is the human contact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the five years to move from pure coding to work close to hospitals, maybe a master's in health informatics part-time. I'd save a deposit with Kit and Lena for a place to buy together. And I'd talk to my boss about making me the person who explains the systems to the clinics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see the road. Five is a number I can plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why health informatics and not something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the rules around patient data are heavy, and somebody has to be accountable. A hospital won't let a machine sign off on who sees a record, at least not early on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if you're wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'll have a master's and a deposit, and I can still start something else. I'd rather be wrong with a plan than right without one.

say: I'd say five years is **long enough** to do something sensible if we start now.
I'd push my firm to run **retraining** and share the savings.
think: By 2031 I might work where **trust matters**, like hospitals, and human contact survives.
I'm **anxious but organised**, and five years is a number I can plan around.
do: Start a part-time master's in **health informatics** and become the person who explains systems to clinics.
Save a flat **deposit** with Kit and Lena.
feel: **Anxious**, but I can see the road.
S3.quote: A hospital won't let a machine sign off on who sees a record, at least not early on.
fieldNote: She links her degree to **trust and accountability** in health data, a plan grounded in her job.
She would rather be wrong with a plan than right without one.
Mood is anxious, not alarmed, because she expects some control.

steps.text: Start a part-time master's in health informatics
Offer to explain the data systems to the partner clinics
Save a deposit with Kit and Lena for a place to buy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is the version where politics can still work. I'd campaign for the rules, for a public stake in the tools and for a shorter working week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fairly calm. By 2036 I'll be 32, and I think I'd be somewhere between engineering and policy. Ten years is long enough to change fields twice if I have to, and I like change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at the startup for a couple of years, then move to a bigger firm or the health service's digital team. I'd study part-time, maybe policy, and keep my open-source project alive. I'd also put 400 a month into a pension, which my mum keeps nagging about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. It's the one where I imagine being a person who got to help design it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame if it goes badly in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The few companies that own it, and the governments who let them. Not the engineers, mostly, though I'd count myself in the group that should have asked louder questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What question would you ask first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who owns the thing, and who gets paid when it works. It's a boring question and nobody wants to answer it.

say: I'd say ten years is when **politics can still work**.
I'd campaign for rules, a **public stake** and a shorter working week.
think: By 2036 I'll be 32 and somewhere between **engineering and policy**.
I like change, and ten years lets me **change fields twice** if I have to.
do: Stay at the startup a couple of years, then move to the health service's **digital team**.
Study **policy** part-time and pay 400 a month into a pension.
feel: **Calm** and curious; I'd get to help design it.
S4.quote: Who owns the thing, and who gets paid when it works. It's a boring question and nobody wants to answer it.
fieldNote: She blames the **few firms** that own the tools and the governments who let them, in line with her outlook.
She includes herself in the group that should have asked **louder questions**.
Ten years makes her the calmest here, because she likes change.

steps.text: Stay at the startup two more years and then apply to the health service digital team
Campaign for a public stake in AI and a shorter week

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Two years, definitely. It's the one where I'd be alone with a loan and a degree that stopped being worth anything overnight. What would help is a basic income, a public stake in the big systems, and employers who retrain people before they let them go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not scared of the technology. I'm scared of who owns it and who gets paid. I'd like someone in charge to be honest about that.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of the technology. I'm scared of who owns it and who gets paid.
portrait: Rosa is a 22-year-old **software engineer** in her first job at a small Bristol health-tech startup, owing about 20,000.
She is adaptive, uses an **AI assistant** all day, and sees clearly that entry-level coding is the exposed part.
Her progressive outlook means she blames **ownership and power** and backs public stakes, regulation and basic income.
She is alarmed at two years, anxious but organised at five, and **calm** when she has ten.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries her most, because she'd be alone with a loan and a degree that lost its value overnight.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income**, a public stake in the big systems, and employers who retrain people before letting them go.
